name: Adele Goldstine
milestone_by_age_26: Trained the six original ENIAC programmers and wrote the first operating manual for an electronic digital computer at the Moore School, 1945-1946.
early_history_summary: Goldstine earned a Master's in mathematics from the University of Michigan at age 22 and married Herman Goldstine, the ENIAC project administrator, in 1941. She joined the Moore School at UPenn in 1942, taught ballistics to women 'computers,' and by 1945 was training the six women selected as ENIAC's first programmers. She wrote the ENIAC Operators Manual and in 1946 implemented Dick Clippinger's stored-program modification, converting ENIAC to execute fifty stored instructions.
secondary_engine: Network / capital (through husband Herman Goldstine, ENIAC administrator)
family_context_summary: Born to Yiddish-speaking Jewish immigrant parents in New York City; father William Katz was a successful retail businessman who emigrated from Lithuania in 1902.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of parental domain expertise in mathematics or computing; father was a retail businessman.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Moore School, ENIAC project, wartime computing, husband-administrator access
evidence_summary: Goldstine's access to the ENIAC project came through her husband Herman Goldstine, who was the military liaison and administrator for ENIAC construction. She joined the Moore School at UPenn in 1942 and leveraged this position to become one of the first computer programmers in history. Her father was a successful businessman, providing a middle-class upbringing, but the key advantage was her embeddedness in the wartime computing frontier at UPenn. She trained the six original ENIAC programmers and wrote the first manual for an electronic digital computer by age 25-26.
starting_point: Born to a Jewish immigrant family in New York City; father William Katz was a successful retail businessman who emigrated from Lithuania in 1902.
current_position: Died in November 1964 at age 43 from cancer; final work was on ENIAC programs for Los Alamos National Laboratory.

trajectory.event: Joined the Moore School of Electrical Engineering at UPenn as a mathematics instructor for women 'computers' calculating ballistic trajectories.
Trained the six original ENIAC programmers and wrote the ENIAC operating manual, the first manual for an electronic digital computer.
Implemented Dick Clippinger's stored-program modification enabling ENIAC to execute fifty stored instructions without manual rewiring.
Worked on ENIAC programs for the Los Alamos National Laboratory, applying the computer to nuclear weapons calculations.
Died of cancer in November 1964.

name: Mary K. Hawes
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Hawes proposed the need for a common business language (leading to COBOL) in March 1959 at age 31-32, well past the age-26 cutoff.
early_history_summary: Hawes worked as a senior product planning analyst at Burroughs Corporation's ElectroData Division. Her key contribution — identifying the need for COBOL and initiating the CODASYL process — occurred in 1959 when she was in her early thirties. No documented achievements by age 26 (1953) were found.
evidence_summary: No biographical details about Hawes's early life, education, or career before 1959 were found in reviewed sources. Her documented achievement — initiating the COBOL development process — occurred in 1959 at age 31-32, past the age-26 cutoff.

name: Jean Sammet
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Sammet wrote a 20-line SPEEDAC loader in January 1955 at age 26, but this was minor; her material milestone — co-developing COBOL — came in 1959 at age 31.
early_history_summary: Sammet earned a BA in mathematics from Mount Holyoke in 1947 (age 19) and an MA from the University of Illinois in 1949 (age 21). She worked as a mathematician at Sperry Gyroscope from 1953 and began programming the SPEEDAC in January 1955. Her co-development of COBOL occurred in 1959 at Sylvania Electric Products, and she developed FORMAC at IBM in 1962.
family_context_summary: Born in New York City to Harry and Ruth Sammet, who were both lawyers. She attended public elementary schools in Manhattan.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were lawyers; no direct technology or computing domain expertise in the family.
evidence_summary: Sammet's early programming work (SPEEDAC loader, January 1955, age 26) was a minor 20-line program, not a material milestone. Her independently verifiable material achievement — co-developing COBOL — came in 1959 at age 31. She was barred from attending Bronx High School of Science because it did not accept girls, attending Julia Richman High School instead.

name: Erna Schneider Hoover
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Hoover earned her PhD from Yale in 1951 at age 25 and taught at Swarthmore, but her material invention — computerized telephone switching — came at Bell Labs in the 1960s, with the patent granted in 1971.
early_history_summary: Hoover earned a BA from Wellesley in 1948 (age 22) and a PhD in philosophy and foundations of mathematics from Yale in 1951 (age 25). She taught at Swarthmore College from 1951-1953, then joined Bell Labs in 1954 (age 28). Her invention of stored program control for telephone switching came in the late 1950s-1960s, with the patent granted in 1971.
family_context_summary: Born in Irvington, New Jersey; father was a dentist and mother was a teacher. She had a younger brother who died of polio at age five.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of parental domain expertise in computing or mathematics; father was a dentist, mother a teacher.
evidence_summary: Hoover's PhD from Yale at age 25 was standard academic progression, not a material career milestone. Her independently verifiable material achievement — the computerized telephone switching system — was developed at Bell Labs starting in 1954 (age 28) with the patent granted in 1971. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Karen Spärck Jones
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Spärck Jones co-authored a paper in the 1958 ICISI proceedings at age 23, but her material achievement — introducing IDF term weighting — came in the 1960s, and her PhD was completed in 1964 at age 29.
early_history_summary: Spärck Jones was an undergraduate at Girton College, Cambridge from 1953-1956. She started research at the Cambridge Language Research Unit in the late 1950s, co-authoring a paper in the 1958 International Conference on Scientific Information. Her PhD thesis 'Synonymy and Semantic Classification' was completed in 1964, and her introduction of IDF term weighting came in the 1960s.
family_context_summary: Born in Huddersfield, Yorkshire; father Alfred Owen Jones was a chemistry lecturer, mother Ida Spärck was a Norwegian who worked for the Norwegian government in exile in London during WWII.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a chemistry lecturer, providing an academic household environment, but no direct computing or NLP domain expertise.
evidence_summary: Spärck Jones's 1958 co-authored conference paper at age 23 is documented but is not a clearly material individual milestone. Her independently verifiable material achievement — IDF term weighting, foundational to modern search engines — came in the 1960s after age 26. Her PhD was completed in 1964 at age 29.

name: Adele Goldberg
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Goldberg earned her BA in 1967 (age 22) and MS in 1969 (age 24), but her material achievement — co-developing Smalltalk at Xerox PARC — began in 1973 when she was 28.
early_history_summary: Goldberg earned a BA in mathematics from the University of Michigan in 1967, an MS in information science from the University of Chicago in 1969, and a PhD in 1973. She worked briefly as a research assistant at Stanford and as a professor in Rio de Janeiro before joining Xerox PARC in 1973 as a research scientist, where she co-developed Smalltalk-80 with Alan Kay and Dan Ingalls.
family_context_summary: Born in Cleveland, Ohio; family moved to Chicago when she was 11. Teachers encouraged her to pursue mathematics. Not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Goldberg's material achievement — co-developing Smalltalk-80 and advancing object-oriented programming at Xerox PARC — began in 1973 when she was 28, past the age-26 cutoff. Her PhD was also completed in 1973. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Wendy Hall
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Hall earned her BSc in 1974 (age 22) and PhD in mathematics in 1977 (age 25), but her material achievement — the Microcosm hypermedia system — came in the mid-1980s when she was in her thirties.
early_history_summary: Hall was born in west London and educated at Ealing Grammar School for Girls. She earned a BSc in mathematics from the University of Southampton in 1974 and a PhD in mathematics (on Klein surfaces) in 1977. She later completed an MSc in Computing at City University London before returning to Southampton in 1984 to join the computer science group, where she led the development of the Microcosm hypermedia system.
family_context_summary: Born in west London; educated at Ealing Grammar School for Girls. Not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Hall's PhD in mathematics at age 25 was standard academic progression. Her material achievement in computer science — the Microcosm hypermedia system, a forerunner to the World Wide Web — was developed in the mid-1980s when she was in her early thirties, well past the age-26 cutoff.

name: Judith Estrin
milestone_by_age_26: No clearly datable material milestone by age 26 found. Estrin worked on TCP testing at Stanford (1976-77, age 23-24) as a student assistant and managed Zilog's ZNet product (introduced June 1980, age 26-27 depending on birth date), but her birth year is uncertain (1953 per CSV; 1954 per Wikidata; 1954/1955 per Wikipedia) and neither achievement is clearly material at an independently verifiable age at or before 26.
early_history_summary: Estrin earned a BS in math and computer science from UCLA and an MS in electrical engineering from Stanford in 1977. She worked under Vint Cerf on TCP testing at Stanford, then joined Zilog where she managed development of the ZNet networking product (introduced June 1980). She co-founded Bridge Communications in 1981 and later co-founded seven more companies, serving as CTO of Cisco Systems from 1998-2000.
evidence_summary: Estrin's TCP work at Stanford was as a student research assistant under Vint Cerf, not a primary individual contribution. The ZNet product at Zilog (June 1980) may have been at age 26 or 27 depending on her uncertain birth year. Her first company co-founding (Bridge Communications, 1981) was at age 27-28. Given the birth year uncertainty and the conservative scoring approach, no clearly material milestone at or before age 26 was established.

name: Sandy Lerner
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Lerner earned her BA in 1975 and MA in 1977, but her material achievement — co-founding Cisco Systems — came in 1984 at age 29 (per CSV birth year) or 32 (per some sources).
early_history_summary: Lerner earned a BA in political science from California State University, Chico in 1975, an MA in econometrics from Claremont Graduate School in 1977, and an MS in statistics and computer science from Stanford in 1981. She became Director of Computing Services at Stanford's Graduate School of Business. She co-founded Cisco Systems with then-husband Len Bosack in 1984, commercializing multi-protocol routers they built at Stanford.
family_context_summary: Born in California circa 1952-1955 (sources differ); parents divorced when she was four. She split childhood between a cattle ranch in the California Sierras and Beverly Hills. She bought her first steer at age nine and built a registered livestock herd of 30 head by college, funding her tuition.
parent_family_domain_summary: No evidence of parental technology or business domain expertise; parents divorced early. Lerner developed entrepreneurial instincts independently through cattle ranching.
evidence_summary: Lerner's material achievement — co-founding Cisco Systems and pioneering commercial routing technology — came in 1984 when she was 29-32 (sources differ on birth year), well past the age-26 cutoff. Her earlier degrees and Stanford computing role were standard career progression, not material milestones.

name: Len Bosack
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Bosack graduated from UPenn in 1973 (age 21) and worked at DEC as a hardware engineer before joining Stanford in 1979 (age 27). His material achievement — co-founding Cisco Systems — came in 1984 at age 32.
early_history_summary: Bosack graduated from La Salle College High School in 1969 and from the University of Pennsylvania in 1973. He joined DEC as a hardware engineer, then was accepted to Stanford University in 1979 to study computer science. At Stanford, he worked as a support engineer on a 1981 project to connect Stanford's networks, and developed the multi-protocol router with Sandy Lerner. They co-founded Cisco Systems in 1984.
family_context_summary: Born in Pennsylvania in 1952 to a Polish Catholic family. Not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Bosack's material achievement — co-founding Cisco Systems and pioneering commercial routing technology — came in 1984 at age 32, well past the age-26 cutoff. His work at DEC (1973-1979) and early Stanford networking work (1979-1981) were standard career progression before the age-26 cutoff.

name: Andy Bechtolsheim
category: Hardware engineer / tech entrepreneur (Sun Microsystems, Arista Networks)
milestone_by_age_26: Designed and built the first SUN workstation at Stanford University, with a working prototype by November 30, 1980 at age 25; co-founded Sun Microsystems in February 1982 at age 26.
early_history_summary: Bechtolsheim grew up on an isolated farm in Bavaria with no television, experimenting with electronics from childhood. At age 16, he designed an industrial controller based on the Intel 8008 for a local company, earning royalties that funded his education. He won the Jugend forscht physics prize in 1974, earned an engineering degree from TU Munich, an MS from Carnegie Mellon in 1976 (age 20), and became a PhD student at Stanford in 1977. Inspired by the Xerox Alto at PARC, he designed the SUN workstation at Stanford, with the first prototype built by November 1980.
family_context_summary: Born on an isolated farm in Bavaria, Germany; father was an elementary school teacher, mother a housewife. Family had minor nobility title (Freiherr/Baron) but was not affluent. Bechtolsheim is the only engineer in his extended family, with the exception of a great-great-uncle who invented the milk centrifuge.
parent_family_domain_summary: No parental domain expertise in engineering or computing; father was a school teacher. The family's noble title did not translate to financial advantage.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught electronics, early microprocessor access, Xerox PARC exposure, Stanford PhD, Silicon Valley
evidence_summary: Bechtolsheim's path was driven by self-created domain repetition from childhood — taking apart radios at age four, building electronics in his parents' basement, and designing a commercial industrial controller at 16. His access to the Intel 8008 as a teenager in rural Germany was unusual for the era and place. The key institutional advantages came later: a Fulbright scholarship to Carnegie Mellon, Stanford PhD program, and a consulting role at Xerox PARC where he experienced the Alto. He designed the SUN workstation using commodity parts, with a working prototype by November 1980 at age 25, and co-founded Sun Microsystems in February 1982 at age 26.
starting_point: Born on an isolated farm in Bavaria, Germany to a school teacher father and housewife mother; minor nobility family (Freiherr) but not affluent; no television or close neighbors.
current_position: Co-founder and chairman of Arista Networks; net worth estimated at approximately $30 billion; resides in Nevada; remains a German national.

trajectory.event: Designed an industrial controller based on the Intel 8008 microprocessor for a local electronics company, earning royalties that funded much of his education.
Won the physics prize in the Jugend forscht national young researchers competition in Germany.
Earned a master's degree in computer engineering from Carnegie Mellon University on a Fulbright scholarship.
Built the first SUN workstation prototype at Stanford University by November 30, 1980, creating an affordable 32-bit workstation with graphics and networking.
Co-founded Sun Microsystems with Vinod Khosla, Scott McNealy, and Bill Joy to commercialize the SUN workstation design.
Co-founded Granite Systems, a gigabit Ethernet switching company later acquired by Cisco for $220 million.
Made a $100,000 early investment in Google, becoming one of the company's first investors.
Co-founded Arista Networks, a high-speed datacenter and cloud networking company.
Serving as chairman of Arista Networks with an estimated net worth of approximately $30 billion.

name: Vinod Khosla
category: Tech entrepreneur / venture capitalist (Sun Microsystems, Khosla Ventures)
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Daisy Systems, a pioneering electronic design automation company, in January 1981 at age 25-26, serving as its first full-time founder and CFO.
early_history_summary: Khosla grew up in an Indian Army household in New Delhi with no business or technology connections. Inspired by reading about Intel's founding at age 16, he attended IIT Delhi from 1971-1976, where he started the institute's first computer club and wrote a paper on parallel processing. After a failed soy milk startup attempt in India, he earned an MS in biomedical engineering from Carnegie Mellon and an MBA from Stanford in 1979-1980. He co-founded Daisy Systems in January 1981, then co-founded Sun Microsystems in 1982.
family_context_summary: Born to a Punjabi Indian family in Pune; father was an officer in the Indian Army posted to New Delhi. Middle-class household with no business or technology connections. Father wanted him to join the army.
parent_family_domain_summary: No parental domain expertise in technology or business; father was an army officer. No inherited business or technology network.
primary_early_advantage_tags: IIT Delhi, Carnegie Mellon, Stanford GSB, Silicon Valley, no family connections
evidence_summary: Khosla's path was defined by elite institutional pipelines — IIT Delhi (one of the most selective engineering schools in the world), Carnegie Mellon, and Stanford GSB — combined with self-driven entrepreneurial ambition from age 16. He had no family business or technology connections; his father was an army officer. He started IIT Delhi's first computer club and attempted a soy milk startup in India before coming to the US. His co-founding of Daisy Systems in January 1981 at age 25-26 was his first material milestone, followed by co-founding Sun Microsystems in 1982 at age 27.
starting_point: Born to a middle-class Punjabi family in Pune, India; father was an Indian Army officer with no business or technology connections, posted to New Delhi.
current_position: Founder of Khosla Ventures; billionaire with estimated net worth of $5-8 billion; leading an offer to purchase the Seattle Seahawks as of 2026.

trajectory.event: Read about the founding of Intel in Electronic Engineering Times and decided to become a technology entrepreneur; enrolled at IIT Delhi.
Graduated from IIT Delhi with a BTech in electrical engineering; started the institute's first computer club and wrote a paper on parallel processing.
Graduated with an MBA from the Stanford Graduate School of Business, entering Silicon Valley.
Co-founded Daisy Systems, a pioneering electronic design automation company, serving as first full-time founder and CFO.
Co-founded Sun Microsystems with Andy Bechtolsheim, Scott McNealy, and Bill Joy, serving as founding CEO.
Joined Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers as a general partner, beginning a legendary venture capital career.
Founded Khosla Ventures to back disruptive technology-driven companies.
Leading Khosla Ventures with an estimated net worth of $5-8 billion; entered a binding agreement to purchase the Seattle Seahawks.
